p.title: Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports

ext.title: Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports
ext.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2504.15333v1 [cs.CY] (21 Apr 2025); manuscript formatted for PNAS and marked DRAFT. Metadata hint confirmed; author list corrected to full names.
ext.document_type: arXiv preprint (empirical measurement paper with dataset release; PNAS-format draft)
ext.identification: No causal identification strategy. Firm-size and stage results are conditional associations. The paper frames them as associations that call for further study. Stage timing relies on an assumption: lobbying in a quarterly report is directed at the bill's most recent legislative stage, with the report deadline used as the timing proxy (p.5).
ext.coverage: Full text read: every line of the extracted text (about 3,280 numbered lines), covering main text pp.1-9, references 1-34, and SI Appendices 1-6 (Tables 2-21, Figs 7-12). Both annotation files were read in full: E = ef8b6c693fc3.json (99 highlights) and A = a60235faab0f.json (112 highlights plus 1 free-text note). Both are authored by Paul Goff and overlap heavily, so paul_markup groups items by passage; every E and A index is accounted for. Highlight colour meaning is not recorded in the files (Y = yellow, G = green, P = pink, B = blue). Covered text is paraphrased, not quoted, to respect the copyright limit. Extraction artifacts (stray tokens such as FT, DRA, RAF, and split words) are treated as text-layer noise.
ext.research_question: Can the positions that U.S. interest groups take on individual bills (Support, Oppose, or Engage, where Engage = Amend + Monitor) be measured directly from Lobbying Disclosure Act reports across all bills from the 111th to 117th Congresses? The paper then asks how those positions vary by legislative stage, firm size, bill subject, and industry.
ext.theory: No formal model is stated. Framing draws on cited work: lobbying as a legislative subsidy (ref 3); firm size shapes corporate political activity through fixed and variable costs, affecting both whether firms lobby and which positions they take (refs 30, 31); lobbying varies by legislative stage (refs 27, 28; ex post lobbying, ref 29); legislative and lobbying networks predict political activity (refs 14, 21); latent preferences are estimated from positions the way roll-call ideal points are (refs 22, 23); donation-based ideology measures may not reflect expressed policy stances (refs 17, 18).
ext.data: Sample: LDA quarterly lobbying reports filed 2009-2022 (111th-117th Congresses), collected from the Senate Office of Public Records and linked to bill metadata from Congress.gov. About 1.4 million bill-line text pairs before a keyword filter. Final dataset: 279,104 bill positions; 12,032 interest groups; 42,475 bills. Unit: interest group x bill pair. LLM-labelled set: 82,421 positions (6,495 groups; 22,820 bills). GNN-labelled set: 196,683 positions (11,185 groups; 36,824 bills), about 70.5% of all positions. Validation: 391 samples on which two human coders agreed; 1,182 interest group-bill pairs overlap MapLight. GNN training: 22,635 MapLight pairs (18,180 Support, 4,455 Oppose). LPscore sample: 1,796 groups and 2,020 bills. Firm analysis: Compustat firm-year data, 2009-2022, 5,421-7,014 firms per year. CFscore comparison: 218 identically named groups. Bill final-status counts (Table 13, SI p.14): Enacted 715 bills (3,640 groups); Vetoed 3 bills (162 groups); Passed 28 bills (128 groups); Provisionally Killed 74 bills (473 groups).
ext.method: (1) LLM labelling: GPT-4 via Azure OpenAI at temperature 0, zero-shot prompt with bill ID, short and official titles, and lobbying text. Five labels in the LLM stage (Support, Oppose, Amend, Monitor, Mention); Mention covers ambiguous or non-amending activity. (2) GNN refinement: heterogeneous GraphSAGE (SI Table 9: 3 classes, hidden size 90, ELU, dropout 0.2, concat decoder) predicts the interest group-bill link type (Support, Oppose, Engage). Amend and Monitor are merged into Engage because four-class accuracy on Amend was low. Training uses LLM labels plus MapLight labels, with a 7:1:2 split. Seventeen graph configurations are compared (base graph; add sponsors, legislators, registrants, lobbyists, related bills, and combinations); the best is base graph + legislator-lobbyist. Predictions are kept as proxy labels only when class probability exceeds 0.9. (3) LPscores: graded-response IRT (Samejima; R mirt) on Support and Oppose labels, with Engage excluded, after keeping groups with at least 10 bills and bills with at least 10 groups. (4) Analyses: descriptive position shares by legislative stage (Fig 2; stage timing proxied by quarterly report deadline); logistic regression for the decision to lobby and Dirichlet regression for position composition, with predicted-probability differences between firms at the 90th and 10th employment percentiles (Fig 3; year FE; optional NAICS FE, PPENT, COGS; SI Tables 19-20); descriptive position ratios by subject (Fig 4, SI Table 21); LPscore distributions by industry (Fig 5); bill-level latent-score scatter and KDE (Fig 6); Pearson correlation with DIME CFscores (n=218).
ext.scope: Population: U.S. federal interest groups that filed LDA reports on named bills (S. and H.R. bills), 2009-2022 (111th-117th Congresses). Firm analysis: Compustat-listed companies only. Institutions: Congress (committee, floor, enactment, veto stages) and the executive via presidential action. Groups that do not file lobbying reports are outside the dataset, which the paper highlights when comparing with MapLight.

key_findings.finding: Dataset size: 279,104 bill positions across 12,032 interest groups and 42,475 bills. LLM stage yields 82,421 positions and GNN stage yields 196,683.
LLM annotation agrees with two human coders on clear-cut cases.
key_findings.numbers: accuracy 96.93, F1 97.19 on 391 samples where both coders agreed

key_findings.finding: LLM positions match MapLight positions on overlapping pairs.
key_findings.numbers: 1,076 of 1,182 overlapping pairs match (91.03%); MapLight labels only Support and Oppose

key_findings.finding: Best GNN configuration (base graph + legislator-lobbyist), averaged over five seeds.
key_findings.location: Link Type Prediction, p.4; SI Tables 11-12 (SI p.14)
key_findings.numbers: accuracy 78.51 +/- 0.035; F1 74.65; per-class F1 Support 79.19, Oppose 64.06, Engage 80.70; 7:1:2 split; proxy-label threshold 0.9 (Youden cutoff about 0.58 noted, not used)

key_findings.finding: Adding nodes and relations generally raises GNN accuracy and F1; Oppose is the hardest class.
key_findings.location: SI Appendix 2, Best Parameter Result (SI p.12-14)
key_findings.numbers: Base graph accuracy 76.07; best 78.51; Oppose F1 in the 60s across configurations

key_findings.finding: The paper's dataset covers far more groups and bills than MapLight once mapped to LDA lobbying records. Only 13.1% of MapLight pairs match.
key_findings.numbers: MapLight 194,479 pairs; 25,382 match (13.1%), covering 2,195 groups and 5,780 bills; this dataset has 12,032 groups and 42,475 bills

key_findings.finding: LPscores are reliable one-dimensional latent positions for groups.
key_findings.numbers: 1,796 groups and 2,020 bills; EAP reliability 0.95; standard errors 0.03 to 0.30 vs threshold 0.32

key_findings.finding: LPscores and DIME CFscores are only weakly correlated.
key_findings.numbers: Pearson r = 0.191 on 218 identically named groups

key_findings.finding: Position mix shifts across legislative stages. Support rises at enactment; Monitor rises after enactment; Oppose and Amend rise after floor passage for bills that later fail.
key_findings.numbers: Enacted bills: Support rises at Enacted stage; Vetoed bills: Oppose and Amend rise after passing the floor. Vetoed sample is only 3 bills (SI Table 13)

key_findings.finding: Larger firms are much more likely to lobby, and larger firms are more likely to choose Monitor. Smaller firms lean toward Oppose and Amend, though by modest margins.
key_findings.numbers: 90th vs 10th percentile of employees: +19.5 pp probability of lobbying; Monitor +4.5 pp; Oppose -1.8 pp; Amend -1.3 pp. Text says no difference for Support.

key_findings.finding: Bill subject shapes position mix. Taxation and Health are Support-heavy; Public lands and Environment are Oppose-heavy; Economics and Armed Forces are Engage-heavy.
key_findings.numbers: Taxation Support 0.833 (239 bills); Health Support 0.789 (342); Public lands Oppose 0.354 (51); Environmental protection Oppose 0.280 (108); Economics and public finance Engage 0.421 (162); Armed forces Engage 0.357 (78)

key_findings.finding: Industry LPscores separate economic and conservative sectors from social-value and progressive sectors. Conflicting pairs sit at opposite ends.
key_findings.numbers: 1,414 groups across 40 industries (of 94 OpenSecrets categories); Republican/Conservative, Anti-Abortion, Gun Rights at top; Democratic/Liberal, Pro-Abortion, Gun Control at bottom

key_findings.finding: Bill-level latent scores: Support clusters where group and bill preferences align, Oppose where they diverge; Republican-sponsored bills sit higher on the bill axis.
key_findings.location: Fig 6 (A), p.8; sponsor-party distribution SI Fig 12 (SI p.20)

key_findings.finding: Engage positions dominate the GNN-labelled set, so Engage-based findings depend heavily on GNN predictions.
key_findings.numbers: 137,023 GNN-labelled Engage positions of 188,639 overall Engage positions (72.6%)

limitations: Stated by authors: Oppose is harder for the GNN because it is less frequent in the data (p.12, SI Table 12 discussion).
Stated by authors: the proxy-label threshold is set at 0.9 for reliability, above the Youden cutoff of about 0.58 (p.4 footnote).
Stated by authors: the stage timing uses the quarterly report deadline as a proxy for lobbying timing, assuming reported efforts target the bill's latest stage (p.5).
Stated by authors: the firm-size results are described as associations that call for further investigation of firm-level factors (p.6).
Stated by authors: 13.1% MapLight match rate is read as most MapLight groups not actively lobbying (p.4). This is interpretive.
Stated by authors: the explanation for late-stage opposition (urgency; media attention) is offered as a suspicion, not tested (p.5).
Stated by authors: the MapLight comparison used the original dataset before excluding conflicting labels (p.4 footnote), so the 91.03% concordance is on pre-exclusion data.

Reader check (not stated by authors): the abstract claims coverage of all introduced bills, but the methods say bills 'are limited to those that are formally enacted as law, specifically Senate and House bills' (p.3). The two statements are inconsistent, and the stage tables include non-enacted bills.
Reader check: the LLM validation sample is the 391 cases where two coders agreed, which selects clear-cut texts and likely overstates accuracy on ambiguous Mention and Amend cases.
Reader check: MapLight pairs both train the GNN and serve as the external concordance benchmark, and the paper does not say whether the 1,182 concordance pairs were held out from training.
Reader check: most positions (70.5%) and most Engage positions are GNN predictions, so validation of the LLM alone does not cover most of the data.

Reader check: SI Table 14 (Enacted) row totals add to 27,767, but the printed grand total is 29,763. SI Table 15 (Vetoed) row totals add to 340, but the printed total is 364. Column sums are not reconciled.
Reader check: Fig 3 caption says errors come from firm-level block bootstrap, while the SI table notes say clustered standard errors. The inference method is not consistent across the text.

Reader check: text says no statistical difference for Support positions (p.6), but SI Table 19 shows Support coefficients significant at the 10% level in two of five specifications (SI p.16). Amend is significant at the 10% level in three of five.
Reader check: Fig 2 caption colours (Support blue, Oppose red, Amend yellow, Monitor green) differ from the body text (green, pink, yellow, purple).
Reader check: SI Table 4 lists model gpt-4-1106-Preview while the main text names GPT-4 (2023-09-01-preview), which is the API version. Reproducibility depends on the model identifier.
Reader check: the Fig 4 caption does not say which annotation set (LLM, GNN, or combined) produces the subject ratios.
measures: Position labels: Support, Oppose, Amend, Monitor, Mention (LLM stage); Support, Oppose, Engage (GNN stage, Engage = Amend + Monitor)
LPscore: graded-response IRT latent score for interest groups, from Support and Oppose labels (Engage excluded)
Bill latent score: latent preference score for bills (Fig 6, Fig 12)
CFscore: DIME campaign-finance ideology score (comparison only)
Firm size: employee count (primary); log employment; PPENT and COGS as controls
Outcome measures: probability of lobbying (logit); composition of positions (Dirichlet); difference in predicted probabilities at 90th vs 10th percentile
Model performance: accuracy, overall F1, per-class F1, Youden index, class-probability threshold 0.9
Agreement and reliability: human-LLM accuracy and F1; LLM-MapLight match rate; Pearson r with CFscores; EAP reliability; IRT standard errors
Bill position ratios (Support, Oppose, Engage) by bill subject and by industry

rel.summary_md:
Kim, Kim, Jeong, Oh and In Song Kim (arXiv 2025, PNAS-format draft) label which way interest groups lean on individual bills, using the free-text bill lines in LDA quarterly reports from 2009 to 2022 (111th-117th Congresses). The pipeline has two stages. GPT-4 at temperature 0 labels keyword-filtered lines, producing 82,421 positions. A heterogeneous GraphSAGE model then fills in where the text is unclear, producing 196,683 more, about 70.5% of the total. The final dataset has 279,104 group-by-bill positions covering 12,032 groups and 42,475 bills, labelled Support, Oppose, or Engage (Engage merges Amend and Monitor). The LLM agrees with human coders 96.9% of the time, but only on the 391 items where both coders agreed. It matches MapLight on 91% of 1,182 overlapping pairs. The GNN reaches 78.5% accuracy, and Oppose is its weakest class (F1 64). On the substance:
- Support rises toward enactment.
- Oppose and Amend rise late in bills that go on to fail. That finding rests on 3 vetoed bills.
- Comparing firms at the 90th and 10th percentiles of size, larger firms are 19.5 pp more likely to lobby and 4.5 pp more likely to Monitor.
- A one-dimensional IRT score for groups (LPscore) correlates only weakly with DIME CFscores (r = 0.19, n = 218).

This matters here because the system has already taken in this dataset and copied its method. It downloaded the Dataverse release, rebuilt Kim's labelling step with Haiku, and benchmarked it against Kim's published labels at natural base rates. On that benchmark, Support and Oppose come out weak (precision 0.42, recall 0.49) and Amend is never recovered. That result led to the standing rule that inferred positions are evidence for retrieval and adjudication, never automatic weights. The paper's real value to Paul is as calibration gold for 2009-2022 and as raw material for per-bill industry conflict, which the system already computes. It is not a feed that can be wired straight into the graph.

bearings.paper_claim: LLM labels agree with human coders at 96.93% accuracy and F1 97.19, but only on the 391 samples where two coders agreed. MapLight concordance is 91.03% on 1,182 pairs and only covers Support/Oppose, and those pairs also trained the GNN. GNN per-class F1: Support 79.19, Oppose 64.06, Engage 80.70.
bearings.paper_location: Validation p.3; Link Type Prediction p.4; SI Tables 11-12
bearings.system_side: Gold-set validation is meant to measure accuracy at natural base rates and on adversarial frames (for example, the 0.571 goldeval figure for DEBATE). The system's own benchmark of the Kim-format Haiku lane uses the 876 pairs that overlap Kim's published end results. It splits Kim's llm and gnn annotation lanes and does no stratification. It reports three-class accuracy carried by the majority Engage class, Support/Oppose precision 0.42 and recall 0.49, and Amend 0 found of 23.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's validation design picks out clear-cut texts, so its headline accuracy does not carry over to Mention, Amend, or ambiguous lines. The system's benchmark compares Haiku with Kim's labels, not with human truth, and 541 of the 876 pairs are GNN-labelled, so the reference set is itself about 78% accurate. Read the system's numbers as agreement with Kim, not as accuracy. Both are UNVERIFIED as accuracy until a human-gold path reproduces them (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Oppose is the hardest class (GNN F1 in the 60s across all 17 graph configurations), because it is rare. Engage dominates the GNN-labelled set: 137,023 of 188,639 Engage labels (72.6%) come from the GNN. Industries with conflicting interests sit at opposite ends of the LPscore axis (Fig 5).
bearings.paper_location: SI Appendix 2 pp.12-14; Table 1 p.3; Analysis 4 p.7 Fig 5
bearings.system_side: Tensor cells on the industry boards are signed by adjudication. Positions in Kim's format are joined only with the basis tag inferred_<variant>. The standing rule is that they serve retrieval and adjudication only, never automatic weights. The bank-column pilot found about 70% of Oppose labels were wrong when checked against primary text, and it signed zero new rows.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds for Oppose labels on finance-sector bills from both GPT-4 and Haiku readers. The paper reports Oppose weakness for the GNN stage. The system observed it for its own LLM lane on 2021-2026 text. Both point the same way, but they are different readers on different eras.

bearings.paper_claim: Bill-level positions show opposing industries on the same bill. On environmental bills, environmental groups Oppose while commercial groups Support. Subject Oppose ratios: Public lands 0.354 (51 bills), Environmental protection 0.280 (108 bills). The paper does not tabulate conflict between industries on a given bill.
bearings.paper_location: Analysis 3 p.6-7 (Fig 4, SI Table 21); Analysis 4 p.7-9 (Fig 5-6)
bearings.system_side: The contested-bills registry is a loader for per-bill counterparty sets that Paul ratifies. No engine consumes it; the bundle reads it for display only. Separately, org_stance_priors recomputes ALIGNED, OPPOSED, and UNKNOWN per bill for each pair of directional sectors. It uses Kim's historical label_3_class plus current inferred signs, and it hard-fails if a CCCA anchor bill reads OPPOSED for the bank|credit_union pair.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim's data runs only through the 117th Congress (2022), so it can nominate candidate contested bills from the past and calibrate the alliance-conflict recompute. Current bills depend on the weaker Haiku lane. Admission to the registry stays an owner ruling. An OPPOSED pair from inferred labels is a lead, not a fact.

bearings.paper_claim: Positions are measured as interest group x bill. Legislators and sponsors enter only as context nodes in the GNN graph, and the best configuration adds legislator-lobbyist prior-work ties. The paper never measures a position or contact between a group and a member.
bearings.system_side: The member-year lobbying link maps a client to every sponsor and cosponsor of a lobbied bill. That makes P(joined | lobbied) = 1, so it is REFUTED as influence evidence. build_dyad_signs routes inferred org-bill signs through the same sponsor and cosponsor rosters, counting p_support >= 0.7 as support and <= 0.3 as oppose. efficiency_layers then z-scores the resulting signed_non_cu_opposition_count as one of its contest_index components.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim's measure stops at the bill. Pushing it onto members through the bill roster brings back the circularity the system already refuted, so the dyad counts describe what bills members sponsored, not whom an org targeted. Kim's legislator-lobbyist relation is a revolving-door edge, so influence language is barred on it.

bearings.paper_claim: Measured group positions on named bills for 2009-2022. In the system's own pull of this dataset, credit-union trade associations are among the most directional filers: CUNA 174 Support / 12 Oppose, NAFCU 168 / 23.
bearings.system_side: A bill's CU direction comes from a 60-row hand table (cfpb_bill_directions.csv, Reduce +1 / Expand -1) plus the BILLS table in the R scraper. The member-prior override was rejected (0.839 to 0.770 held-out).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Useful as an external audit of the hand-set direction table, but only for bills in the 111th-117th Congresses that CUNA or NAFCU named in LD-2 lines. 118th and 119th Congress bills would need the Haiku lane (Oppose recall about 0.49). Use it to adjudicate the table, never to overwrite it, under the standing rule.

bearings.paper_claim: Firm size is associated with position type. At the 90th vs 10th employment percentile, larger firms are +19.5 pp more likely to lobby and +4.5 pp more likely to Monitor, with Oppose -1.8 pp and Amend -1.3 pp. These are associations, not causal effects.
bearings.system_side: Clients are classified by name (bank, credit union, other) with NAICS used only as linkage metadata. The system measured that its 22 pinned fintech and crypto firms hold 56 positions over 14 years, with one directional label. Directional positions sit with trade associations.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Kim's sample is Compustat firms with year fixed effects and makes no claim about associations. The system's observation (corporate filers mostly non-directional, associations directional) is consistent with it, but it is a descriptive count, not a replication. A coverage map of directional filers should weight associations, not firms.

bearings.paper_claim: GPT-4 zero-shot labelling reaches 96.93% accuracy on 391 coder-agreed lobbying lines after a keyword filter for stance verbs (support, oppose, amend, and similar).
bearings.system_side: The DEBATE NLI reader scores stance toward credit-union interests in member press releases. Accuracy is 0.839 held-out and 0.571 on the adversarial frame. The main bottleneck is the two-hop valence step, not stance detection.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Does not transfer. Kim's text is filtered to explicit position verbs about a named bill, and the validation set excludes disagreements. Press stance toward CUs needs a target-valence step that Kim's task does not have. Paul's annotation cites the 96.9% as support for LLM stance reading; it is not a benchmark for this reader.

gaps_exposed: There is no human-gold check of the Kim-format lane. All system benchmarks score agreement with Kim's labels, and 541 of the 876 benchmark pairs are Kim GNN predictions, which are about 78% accurate.
Kim positions end at the 117th Congress. Current-Congress coverage depends on the Haiku lane, whose Oppose and Support recall is about 0.49, so per-bill conflict for live bills is weakly measured.

Paul's 'reactive, not predictive' critique is unaddressed. Positions arrive after the quarterly deadline, so they cannot be features in the cosponsor forecaster without leakage controls. The forecaster currently uses no position features.
The positions wiring gap noted in the brain: an lda_rebuild ledger regeneration wipes the position columns, and lobby_position_join is not chained, so downstream priors can go stale silently.

No group-level latent scale (LPscore analogue) exists to place CU, bank, crypto and fintech associations on a shared axis. Such a scale would make 'conflicting industries' measurable, not only adjudicated.
flags: Possible conflict with D-021 and the standing rule that inferred positions are never automatic weights. efficiency_layers.py:175-211 puts signed_non_cu_opposition_z, built from inferred Oppose labels pushed onto members through the sponsor/cosponsor roster (org_stance_priors.py:631-700), into contest_index. That artifact is in run_pipeline and shown on the member desk. It moves no rank, but it is an LDA-derived weight inside a displayed score, and its member mapping is the refuted circular roster join. Paul should rule on whether it stays, is labelled UNVERIFIED, or is removed.

Paul's annotation calls the pipeline something to 'implement directly on an SNA vector graph'. Under D-021 (LDA is an identity source, not an edge or weight source) and the standing rule, Kim positions cannot become graph edges or weights. Flag this; do not recommend it.
Kim's best GNN configuration adds legislator-lobbyist prior-work (revolving-door) relations. If that relation is ever borrowed, influence language is barred on those edges.

The paper's 96.93% headline is measured on coder-agreed items only. Paul's position on melange-stance.debate-nli-classifier and melange-validation.gold-set-and-rank-gate cites it as LLM accuracy without that qualifier.

Internal inconsistencies to cite with care: the abstract says all bills, but the methods say enacted S./H.R. bills; the vetoed-stage pattern rests on 3 bills; SI Table 14/15 totals do not reconcile; the text says Support shows no difference, but SI Table 19 has Support significant at p<.10 in 2 of 5 specifications.

Every figure quoted from the system's benchmark (precision 0.42, recall 0.49, 0 of 23 Amend) is agreement with Kim labels on 876 overlap pairs from 2021-2022, not accuracy against human truth. Keep that window and denominator attached.
rel.paul_alignment: Partly aligned, and partly stale. Paul's three findings (stage, firm size and Monitor, industry alignment) match the paper, though the stage result for failing bills is thin (3 vetoed bills). His call that the paper is a 'foundational pre-built pipeline' has already been acted on. The system downloaded the Dataverse release, rebuilt the labelling prompt on Haiku, and benchmarked it. That benchmark is why the pipeline is NOT used to feed the graph directly. Support and Oppose agreement is weak, and the standing rule plus D-021 keep LDA-derived positions as evidence, not edges or weights. His Weakness 2 (no inter-industry conflict per bill) is accurate about the paper's presentation, but the data allows it. The system already builds per-bill ALIGNED and OPPOSED labels for each sector pair, with a CCCA anchor (org_stance_priors.recompute_alliance_conflict), while the contested-bills registry stays display-only pending his ratifications. His Weakness 1 (reactive, not predictive) still holds and is not addressed. His margin note on conflicting industries is borne out by the industry boards' per-axis divergence. His notes do not record that the pipeline was benchmarked, nor that an inferred-Oppose count now feeds the displayed contest_index.

related.why: Same LDA/LobbyView source keyed by lob_id. The positions dataset joins directly onto LobbyView client and bill tables, which the system ingests.
Cited as ref 14. Its lobbying-network structure motivates the GNN graph of groups, bills and legislators in this paper.
The paper compares LPscores against DIME CFscores and finds r = 0.191 (n = 218): ideology from donations and positions from lobbying measure different behaviour.

Same LobbyView research group. It covers how the lobbying network changes over time, while this paper covers what position each group takes. Its legislator network runs to 2023, past this dataset's 2022 end.
The contested-bills registry's counterparty term cites Romero Moreno. Kim's per-bill Support/Oppose labels could supply the counterparty industries it needs.
Both tie firm size to lobbying behaviour. Huneeus and Kim estimate returns, while Kim et al. find larger firms lobby more and Monitor rather than Oppose.
Both use zero-shot LLM labelling of political text, with validation against human coders.
Both mine LDA congressional lobbying records. Harrison is the introductory pipeline guide; Kim adds position labels at scale.

paul_entries.text:
Kim, Jison, et al. *Measuring Interest Group Positions on Legislation: An AI-Driven Analysis of Lobbying Reports*, 23 Apr. 2025.

Professors from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology use Large Language Models and Graph Neural Networks to analyze and underpin the correlation between lobbying firms, the direction and shape of policy preferences, and ultimately derive insights regarding lobbying strategies and firm behavior. This article is foundational to the current research, as it provides a novel, large-scale, and pre-built data pipeline that can be directly implemented on a social network analysis vector graph, yielding insights into the behavior of competing firms. There are three main findings uncovered by the authors: A strong correlation between the bills' place and the legislative process and the positions taken by the interest group; the firm's size plays a key role in the adoption of monitoring positions; and industries align their efforts on issue-specific stakes. Finally, there are two main weaknesses relevant to the current research. First, this method is reactive rather than predictive due to the time lag between the release of filing reports and current industry positions. Finally, this method doesn’t explicitly highlight conflict between industries over a specific bill, which is vital for political intelligence.
